source_spans.locator: Cognition 69(2), pp.135-178 abstract: features that occupy a causal-parent position in a relational structure are predicted to be more important than their effects.
Same abstract: across natural and artifactual categories, measured causal position correlates positively with feature importance.
Same abstract: experiments manipulating causal position in artificial categories show that causal position, rather than category type by itself, explains differences in feature importance.

conditions: category features participate in an asymmetric causal relational structure
task: judge or use category features in real and artificial category structures

nodes.description: position of a feature within an asymmetric causal relation to other features
degree to which a feature influences judgments about category membership or structure
whether the category belongs to one of the compared broad domain types
experimental change to which features occupy causal-parent versus causal-effect positions

relations.description: feature importance depends on causal position within the represented relational structure
differences in feature importance associated with category type are accounted for by differences in causal position rather than by category type alone
experimentally changing causal position changes which features are treated as more important
